coverage_window.note: UK-focused run covering Saturday 21 November and the night into Sunday 22 November. This was a quiet weekend window and the report says so plainly rather than inflating it: almost nothing genuinely new broke in the 24 hours, so the value of this run is in the calendar, three corrections and one closure, not in novelty. The dominant fact is the deadline board. Five CISA KEV remediation deadlines fall inside 48 hours of this report - VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890, Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466, Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 and SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884 on Monday 23 November, and the Microsoft Outlook zero-day CVE-2026-124194 on Tuesday 24 November. That is why ranks 1, 3, 4 and 5 are all patching entries and why this report leads with action rather than analysis. Rank 1 stays with vCenter for a second day on the calendar rather than on novelty, and the window added three things: Mandiant's CTO has stated publicly that the firm investigated MULTIPLE intrusions through this flaw, which is the first confirmation of real compromise beyond scanning; the published fixed-build list (9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200, 8.0 U3m) contains NO 7.0 release, which corroborates yesterday's single-source no-patch-for-7.0 claim and converts Monday into an isolation decision for every UK estate still on that branch; and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has added its own alert alongside NHS England's CC-4899 and CISA's KEV entry, while Broadcom's advisory reportedly still omits in-the-wild exploitation - so any vendor-severity-driven triage will have scored this as routine. Rank 2 is the genuinely new UK government item and a correction: the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill returns to the Commons on TUESDAY 24 NOVEMBER for consideration of Lords amendments, a date yesterday's run recorded as unconfirmed. Peers defeated the Government twice and inserted a statutory register of hostile state cyber actors; third-party trackers also report a narrowed incident definition, mandatory near-miss reporting dropped, and new vendor-direction and AI-agent powers. Rank 3 promotes Cisco Expressway out of yesterday's combined KEV entry because the window produced the actual intrusion chain: two internet-facing Expressway devices breached, pivot to two internal cluster nodes, then custom Python scripts scanning SMB, SQL Server and WinRM and harvesting credentials from internal GitLab repositories. Patch Expressway and ignore your repositories and you have closed the door and left the keys outside. Rank 4 is the Outlook zero-day and the NHS England alert batch, and it is ranked on a delivery mechanism rather than a CVSS score: CVE-2026-124194 ships through the Office updater, NOT Windows Update, so WSUS, Intune Windows rings and SCCM compliance will all report an estate green while every Outlook client stays vulnerable. Rank 5 carries the week's most dangerous false assurance and widens it: disabling XML-RPC in the Roller admin UI does NOT mitigate CVE-2026-129448, the affected range is 4.0.0 onward rather than 6.1.5 alone, 6.1.7 rather than 6.1.6 is the right target, public PoC code predates the advisory by seven weeks - and CISA's own enrichment record dated 18 November shows SSVC exploitation as 'none' while KEV lists it with a 23 November deadline. Rank 6 is the UK's public confirmation, through General Sir Rob Magowan, of offensive cyber operations against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea, included because the retaliation surface for that disclosure is operators rather than the MoD; it carries the NCSC's 1,831 reported attacks with 80 nationally significant, MI5's 50-plus Iran-linked arrests, and the July 2026 four-day loss of control at a small UK power station that has never been formally attributed. Rank 7 demotes Transport for London from yesterday's rank 2 with no new information in the window - around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers, portal still offline six days on, and still no disclosed initial access vector, which is the criticism to make because other UK bodies cannot check whether they share the weakness. Rank 8 is the UK corporate and NHS supply chain leak-site cluster at deliberately low confidence, because Bitdefender's analysis of N0n's own exposed file server indicates just over 20 real victims against more than 100 listings and 126 entries removed from October's totals - but the listings describe a genuinely new asset class nobody has in their inventory: vector indexes, AI storefront assistant conversation corpora and storefront service identities. Fittleworth Medical, an NHS Dispensing Appliance Contractor handling stoma, continence and wound care data, and Waterman Group, with a claimed password register covering Microsoft 365, Azure, NAS, Dropbox admin and bank access, are the two asymmetric-consequence items there. Rank 9 holds NGINX2Root down a second day and can now explain the quiet: Rapid7's own PoC README warns it will likely fail against servers with multiple concurrent clients, which is what 9.48 million exposed production nginx services are - still no KEV listing, still no confirmed exploitation, and blacklisting the unused SCTP kernel module remains the highest-value five-minute action in this report because the escalation flaw has no CVE and no patch. Rank 10 is the deadline and evidence-quality board, and this week it carries a theme: SAP NetWeaver is KEV-listed with a three-day deadline on a year-old patch while no IOCs, attribution or PoC have been published by anyone; N-able states no customer exploitation while Field Effect reports a working exploit chain against Hotfix 2 and XMRig on production servers; and OpenSSH SSHole is the item most likely to be present and unnoticed because organisations assess SSH exposure against servers rather than Alpine container base images. One item closes: all monitored Optimizely files were clean by 23:11 UTC on 16 November, resolving yesterday's TalkTalk concern - but the HSBC detail stands as the week's most transferable lesson, because its CSP blocked the main malicious script while a backup copy still ran. Three corrections this run: the CSR Bill date, the Roller affected range, and the vCenter 7.0 patch position. Rotated out from yesterday: the RDM refrigeration operation (continuing coverage but no new substance; NCSC advice unchanged - patch, change default credentials, get the devices off the internet), N-able as a standalone entry (folded into rank 10), the European Commission AI-assisted attack (not UK), and the Aurora/William Cook and The Gentlemen/Nvidia claims (folded into rank 8's supplier theme). Also considered and not ranked: the New Zealand Defence Force website intrusion of 20 November (not UK), the 3AM ransomware intrusion against a UK school estate (September attack, disclosed 3 November, no new information), UK Government Investments' 51-official data exposure (last financial year, no November development), the Gibraltar government cloud intrusion (no update since 9-11 November), and ASUS Control Center Express and the Amazon AI-agent MONAI Label finding (no UK angle established). vulnerabilities.title: VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890: CISA KEV Deadline Falls Tomorrow (Monday 23 November) - Mandiant's CTO Confirms Multiple Investigated Intrusions, and the Published Fixed-Build List Contains No 7.0 Release
affected_products: VMware vCenter Server 9.1 - fixed build 9.1.1.0200
VMware vCenter Server 9.0 - fixed build 9.0.2.0200
VMware vCenter Server 8.0 - fixed in 8.0 U3m
VMware vCenter Server 7.0 - NO fixed build appears in the published remediation list; end of general support since October 2025
vCenter components bundled in VMware Cloud Foundation, vSphere Foundation and Telco Cloud products
VMSA-2026-0009 also fixes four further issues in VMware SDDC Manager and VMware Tools for Windows
Vulnerable component: VMware Directory Service (vmdir) - authentication bypass using an alternate path or channel (CVSS 9.8)
vulnerabilities.summary:
Held at rank 1 for a second day, and the reason has changed from novelty to the calendar. The CISA KEV remediation deadline for CVE-2026-123890 is Monday 23 November 2026 - tomorrow. Any UK organisation that decided on Friday to look at this 'next week' has one working day left, and this is the entry to action before anything else in this report.

What the window added. Three things, none of which are new vulnerabilities but all of which change how you should size the response.

First, scale. Mandiant's CTO has stated publicly that the company investigated multiple incidents involving ARMORY CASTLE's exploitation of CVE-2026-123890. That is the only quantification anyone has offered and it is deliberately vague, but it is a material upgrade on 'exploitation observed': it means more than one organisation was actually compromised through this flaw, not merely scanned. No victim count, no sector breakdown and no geography have been published, and Google/Mandiant have not said whether any UK entity is among them. Treat the absence of a UK victim statement as absence of information rather than as reassurance.

Second, and this is the correction worth reading, the vCenter 7.0 question from yesterday's run now has a better answer. Yesterday this feed recorded the no-patch-for-7.0 claim as single-source and told you to check Broadcom's matrix. Rapid7's emergency threat response write-up publishes the fixed builds as 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 and 8.0 U3m. There is no 7.0 build in that list. That is consistent with the single-source claim rather than contradicting it, and it is consistent with 7.0 having left general support in October 2025. The practical consequence for the significant number of UK public sector and NHS estates still running vCenter 7.0: Monday is not a patching decision for you, it is an isolation or acceleration decision, and it needs an owner by close of business. Verify against Broadcom's own advisory matrix before you write the change record - this feed is reading a vendor-adjacent analysis, not the matrix itself.

Third, corroboration breadth. The Canadian Centre for Cyber Security has issued its own alert, which states that open-source reporting indicates exploitation. Combined with NHS England Digital's cyber alert CC-4899 of 19 November - High severity, explicitly citing observed in-the-wild exploitation - and the CISA KEV addition on 20 November with a three-day deadline, there are now three national cyber authorities carrying this. One further detail from the window worth holding onto: at least one source notes Broadcom's advisory still does not mention in-the-wild exploitation. If your patching process is driven by vendor advisory severity alone, it will have scored this as an ordinary critical. It is not one.

The mechanism and the chain, restated because the deadline makes it urgent. CVE-2026-123890 is a critical authentication bypass in the VMware Directory Service, the component underpinning vCenter Single Sign-On, reachable by a remote unauthenticated attacker who can thereby obtain an administrator session. Exploitation by ARMORY CASTLE - formerly tracked as UNC5221, suspected PRC-nexus espionage - began as early as September 2026, more than two months before Broadcom shipped the fix on 19 November. Mandiant reports evidence the group knew of the flaw before 29 July 2026, the disclosure date of CVE-2026-59309, a separate vCenter authentication bypass. In the intrusion Mandiant describes, initial access came not through vCenter but through a BeyondTrust zero-day, CVE-2026-102764, after which the actor moved laterally to internal Linux appliances that lacked EDR coverage. Against vCenter the group used BONESAW, a custom Go utility with a 13 July 2026 build timestamp, which extracted /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb, obtained SAML Security Token Service signing material and created an SSO administrator account. Reconnaissance used nmap against ports 443, 2012, 5480 and 9080. Follow-on tooling: SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES, SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH, all with YARA rules published by Google Threat Intelligence.

Why patching does not close this. If you were reachable and unpatched between early September and 19 November, the question is not your patch state, it is whether someone was already inside for ten weeks. Theft of STS signing material is the detail that should set your severity: an attacker who can sign their own SAML assertions can mint authenticated sessions across every service trusting that identity provider, and no password reset revokes that capability. Rotating signing material is disruptive, which is precisely why the decision needs taking now rather than discovering later.

Confidence and caveats. High on the identifier, CVSS, vmdir component, 19 November patch date, VMSA-2026-0009, the 20 November KEV addition with 23 November deadline, the ARMORY CASTLE attribution, the BONESAW tradecraft and the fixed-build numbers. The 'multiple incidents' statement is attributed to Mandiant's CTO via secondary coverage and carries no numbers. The absence of a 7.0 build is an inference from a published remediation list, not a vendor statement that no fix will come. Google/Mandiant file hashes and YARA rule contents were NOT retrieved in this run - every direct page fetch failed on DNS resolution, as it did yesterday - so the indicators below remain behavioural only. One source states there is no public exploit; treat that as perishable.
recommended_actions: Today or first thing Monday: patch vCenter to 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 or 8.0 U3m as an emergency change. The CISA KEV deadline is Monday 23 November. If you have not started, this is the one item in this report that should displace other work.

If you run vCenter 7.0, stop treating this as a patch. No 7.0 build appears in the published fixed-release list and the branch left general support in October 2025. Confirm against Broadcom's advisory matrix, then assign an owner on Monday for either isolation behind a jump host with no routable path from user VLANs, or an accelerated upgrade. Record the decision - an unremediated internet- or LAN-reachable 7.0 vCenter is now a documented risk acceptance, not an oversight.

Run the compromise hunt regardless of patch state, scoped to early September onward. Mandiant has now confirmed it investigated multiple real intrusions through this flaw; the base rate is no longer theoretical. Scope the hunt to vCenter, ESXi, SDDC Manager and adjacent Linux appliances, not vCenter alone.

Enumerate every vCenter SSO administrator account in vsphere.local and reconcile against approved change records. BONESAW was observed creating one. An account you cannot tie to an approved change is an incident, not a finding.

Decide this week whether to rotate SAML Security Token Service signing material on any vCenter you cannot positively clear. An attacker holding STS signing keys can mint valid assertions for everything that trusts that identity provider; password resets do not revoke it.
Check for any access to, or copy of, /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb outside its normal path. Exfiltration of the vmdir database is the observed objective.

Pull the full indicator set and YARA rules directly from the Google Cloud / Mandiant ARMORY CASTLE publication and load rules for BONESAW, SAWSNAKE, BEARBONES, LAZYBONES, SLIMSAVAGE and CAGEMATCH. The IOCs in this entry are behavioural; hashes were not retrievable in this run.

Do not let your vendor-advisory-driven patch triage decide this one. Broadcom's advisory reportedly still omits in-the-wild exploitation, so severity-only scoring will have ranked it as routine. CISA, NHS England Digital and the Canadian Centre for Cyber Security have all now said otherwise.

Inventory every appliance in the estate - virtualisation, backup, identity, remote access, building management - and record whether it carries EDR. The reported intrusion reached vCenter through internal Linux appliances with no EDR coverage. That inventory outlasts this CVE.

Check your BeyondTrust estate against CVE-2026-102764, the reported initial-access leg, and resolve it against the vendor advisory rather than a scanner product string - this feed recorded a product-matching dispute on that identifier on 17 October.

NHS organisations: CC-4899 is dated 19 November with High severity. If it is still open in your queue on Monday morning with the KEV deadline that day, escalate it rather than working it in date order.

kql.name: vCenter SSO administrator account creation - ARMORY CASTLE / BONESAW
kql.description: Primary detection. BONESAW was observed creating an SSO administrator account on compromised vCenter appliances. Lookback deliberately exceeds the early-September exploitation start. Requires vCenter appliance syslog forwarding.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "vsphere")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("vmdird", "vmdir", "sso", "vmware-sts", "vmafd")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Add entry", "CreateUser", "user created", "added to group", "Administrators@vsphere.local", "member add")
| extend Principal = extract(@"(?:cn=|user[ =:])([A-Za-z0-9._\-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SeverityLevel, Principal, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Access to or copy of the vmdir database file data.mdb
kql.description: BONESAW extracted /storage/db/vmware-vmdir/data.mdb to obtain directory contents and SAML STS signing material. Any read, copy or archive of that path by a process other than vmdird is suspicious.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has "data.mdb" or SyslogMessage has "vmware-vmdir"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("cp ", "tar", "scp", "curl", "wget", "gzip", "base64", "dd if=", "cat ", "rsync")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Reconnaissance against the vCenter management port set (443, 2012, 5480, 9080)
kql.description: ARMORY CASTLE conducted nmap reconnaissance against vCenter and adjacent service ports before exploitation. Distinct-port fan-out from a single internal source is the signal, not the individual connection.
kql.query:
let lookback = 120d;
let vcPorts = dynamic([443, 2012, 5480, 9080, 8089, 7444]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort in (vcPorts)
| summarize DistinctPorts = dcount(DestinationPort), PortList = make_set(DestinationPort, 10), DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), Attempts = count()
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctPorts >= 3 or DistinctTargets >= 5
| order by Attempts desc

kql.name: Anomalous federated sign-in after suspected STS signing material theft
kql.description: If STS signing material was stolen the attacker can mint valid assertions. Hunt federated sign-ins with no corresponding device or with improbable location spread. Hunting query - tune heavily before any alerting use.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
AADNonInteractiveUserSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where AuthenticationProtocol has_any ("saml", "wsFederation")
| extend Dev = tostring(DeviceDetail.deviceId), Loc = tostring(LocationDetails.countryOrRegion)
| summarize SignIns = count(), Countries = make_set(Loc, 10), Devices = dcount(Dev) by UserPrincipalName, AppDisplayName
| where Devices == 0 or array_length(Countries) > 2
| order by SignIns desc

kql.name: vCenter build version inventory for KEV deadline evidence (23 November)
kql.description: Deadline support query. Surfaces logged build/version strings so you can evidence which appliances reached 9.1.1.0200, 9.0.2.0200 or 8.0 U3m, and which are still on 7.0 with no fixed build published.
kql.query:
let lookback = 14d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "vsphere", "sddc")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("build", "version", "vpxd", "appliance version")
| extend Build = extract(@"(\d+\.\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(Build)
| summarize LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Builds = make_set(Build, 10) by Computer
| extend KnownFixed = iff(Builds has_any ("9.1.1.0200", "9.0.2.0200"), "fixed-build-seen", "verify-against-VMSA-2026-0009")
| order by Computer asc

kql.name: Go binaries and archive staging on virtualisation management hosts
kql.description: BONESAW is a Go utility (build timestamp 13 July 2026). Hunt unexpected statically linked binaries and staging activity on or adjacent to virtualisation management infrastructure.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceName has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "esxi", "vsphere", "sddc")
    or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any ("/tmp/", "/var/tmp/", "/dev/shm/")
| where FileName in~ ("tar", "gzip", "zip", "base64", "openssl", "curl", "wget", "nc", "socat")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("data.mdb", "vmware-vmdir", "/storage/db/")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Outbound connections from virtualisation appliances
kql.description: Appliances should not initiate arbitrary outbound connections. Surfaces egress from management-plane hosts - the exact place the reported intrusion's EDR coverage gap would have shown.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where DeviceName has_any ("vcenter", "vcsa", "esxi", "vsphere", "sddc", "nsx")
| where ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP
| order by Connections desc

vulnerabilities.summary:
This is the highest-value genuinely new UK government item in the window, and it is a correction. Yesterday's run recorded the Cyber Security and Resilience Bill as sitting at Commons consideration of Lords amendments with 'no November date confirmed'. The date is now confirmed by the House of Commons Library: the Bill has completed its Lords stages and is scheduled to return to the Commons on Tuesday 24 November 2026 for consideration of Lords amendments. That is in two days.

Why a parliamentary date belongs in a threat intelligence report. Because this Bill is the instrument that will decide, for every UK operator of essential services, what counts as a reportable incident, how fast you must report it, who your regulator is, and whether your suppliers are in scope. Two days from now the Commons starts deciding which of the Lords' changes survive. If your organisation has a position on any of the items below, the window to make it known to a regulator, trade body or parliamentarian is roughly 48 hours, and it closes for good once ping-pong concludes.

The Lords stages, as evidenced. Committee stage concluded Monday 7 September. Report stage completed 26 October, where amendments were considered on voluntary incident notification, bringing service providers and software manufacturers inside the NIS framework, and designating critical suppliers. Third reading was scheduled for and reportedly completed on 2 November. Peers held three divisions on proposed changes and the Government lost two of them. The successful amendments require the Government to maintain a register of state actors posing a threat to UK cyber security; a third-party tracker characterises the two defeats as a review of the whole NIS regime and a foreign powers register.

The substantive changes to watch on Tuesday, with a confidence warning attached. A third-party guide - not Parliament - reports that the Lords narrowed the incident definition, dropped mandatory near-miss reporting, added customer update obligations, added vendor directions and AI-agent powers, and inserted both a regime review and the foreign powers register. Each of those has a direct operational consequence. A narrowed incident definition reduces reporting volume but also reduces the national picture the NCSC can build. Dropping mandatory near-miss reporting removes what would have been a genuinely novel obligation and, for most security teams, the most expensive one to build tooling for. Vendor directions and AI-agent powers are new regulatory surface that did not exist when most organisations wrote their compliance gap analyses. Treat this list as indicative: it is the least well-sourced part of this entry and the Parliament and Commons Library pages are the authoritative record.

A register of hostile state actors is the item worth thinking hardest about. It is attractive in principle and awkward in practice. A statutory UK register naming state actors that threaten UK cyber security creates a public, Government-attested attribution list, which has consequences for insurance, for procurement, for contractual force majeure and for any organisation that must now explain why it continued using a supplier with ties to a listed state. It also creates a diplomatic artefact that the Government will be slow to update, which is why it was resisted. If it survives Tuesday, UK organisations acquire a compliance input they have never had before.

The timing against the rest of this report is not coincidental and is worth stating to a board. In the same seven-day period: a PRC-nexus actor is confirmed to have held undetected access to VMware vCenter estates for ten weeks (rank 1), the head of the UK's Cyber and Specialist Operations Command publicly confirmed offensive operations against four hostile states (rank 6), and a UK government body is managing a live breach of 265,000 transport customers' records (rank 7). The Bill's passage and the threat picture it responds to are moving at the same time.

Confidence and caveats. High confidence on the 24 November Commons date, the completion of Lords stages, the 7 September committee and 26 October report stage dates, the three divisions with two Government defeats, and the hostile-state-actor register as the subject of a successful amendment, all evidenced by Parliament and Commons Library pages. Medium at best on the detailed amendment list, which comes from third-party trackers, some of which are demonstrably stale - one still shows report stage as the current stage with a mid-September last-update. Royal Assent timing is an estimate: one third-party source expects late 2026 to spring 2027, which is not an official timetable. The Bill is cited variously as HL Bill 32, 49 and 62 depending on printing, so match on title rather than number. No direct page fetch succeeded in this run; all of this is from search-surfaced content including Parliament's own pages.
recommended_actions: Put Tuesday 24 November in the diary of whoever owns regulatory compliance, and get the Commons consideration of Lords amendments watched rather than read about afterwards. The decisions taken that day set your reporting obligations.

Re-run your CSRB gap analysis against the amended Bill rather than the version introduced. If your analysis predates 26 October it does not reflect report stage, and if it predates 2 November it does not reflect third reading. A gap analysis against a superseded text is worse than none, because it creates false assurance.

Specifically re-check two assumptions: that you will have to build near-miss reporting (reportedly dropped by the Lords), and that software manufacturers and managed service providers are or are not in your scope chain (actively amended). Both change project scope and budget.

If you are a managed service provider or a plausible 'designated critical supplier', assume you are in scope and start now. Designation is not something you will get much notice of, and the N-able and Optimizely events in this report are exactly the supplier-concentration risk the category exists to address.

Prepare for the hostile-state-actor register as a procurement and supply-chain input, not a security one. If it becomes statutory, your procurement, legal and insurance functions will need a process for screening suppliers against it. Decide now who owns that.

Map the reportedly narrowed incident definition against your current incident classification scheme and identify which of your historical incidents would and would not have been reportable. That exercise tells your board what the regime actually costs you, far better than reading the Bill does.

Note the new vendor direction and AI-agent powers if they survive. Any organisation running autonomous agents against production systems should assume this becomes regulated surface, and should be able to produce an inventory of those agents.

Verify every detail in this entry against the House of Commons Library briefing CBP-10442 and Parliament's own Bill pages before briefing a board or committee. The amendment detail here comes from third-party trackers of mixed reliability, and some are stale.

Do not wait for Royal Assent to start. Estimates range from late 2026 to spring 2027, and the implementation work - asset inventory, incident classification, supplier mapping, reporting pipelines - takes longer than the gap between assent and commencement will give you.

kql.name: Incident classification baseline for the amended CSRB reporting definition

let lookback = 365d;
SecurityIncident
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| summarize Incidents = count(), Closed = countif(Status == "Closed"), MedianHoursToClose = percentile(datetime_diff('hour', ClosedTime, CreatedTime), 50)
    by Severity, Classification = tostring(Classification), bin(TimeGenerated, 30d)

kql.name: Near-miss candidate volume - what mandatory near-miss reporting would have cost

vulnerabilities.title: Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466: KEV Deadline Tomorrow, and the Window Has Produced the Actual Intrusion Chain - Two Internet-Facing Nodes Breached, Pivot to Internal Cluster Members, Then Credential Theft From Internal GitLab Repositories
affected_products: Cisco Expressway-C - clustered deployments only
Cisco Expressway-E - clustered deployments only
Cisco Video Communication Server (VCS) - same advisory family (cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t)
Vulnerable component: cluster database service, Erlang-based, listening on TCP 4372
Fixed release: X15.5.20
Non-clustered Expressway deployments are reported as not affected
vulnerabilities.summary:
Promoted out of yesterday's combined KEV-batch entry to a rank of its own, because the window produced the thing that was missing on Friday: a description of what attackers actually do after they exploit this. Its KEV deadline, like vCenter's, is Monday 23 November.

The flaw. CVE-2026-76466 is a CVSS 9.8 hard-coded credentials vulnerability (CWE-798) in the cluster database service of clustered Cisco Expressway-C and Expressway-E. The service runs on Erlang and listens on TCP 4372. A maintenance identity and its Erlang cookie are compiled into the software and are identical on every single installation, which means there is no credential to rotate and no password policy that helps. Successful exploitation gives command execution as root on the Expressway operating system with no credentials required. The fix is X15.5.20. There is no workaround. Only clustered deployments are affected - if your Expressway pair is standalone, you are reported to be out of scope, which is worth confirming before you schedule emergency downtime on a video platform.

The intrusion chain, which is the new material. Reporting in this window describes attackers first breaching two internet-facing Expressway devices, then pivoting to two further cluster nodes on the internal network. Having landed, they ran custom Python scripts that scanned for SMB shares, probed SQL Server and WinRM, and pulled credentials from internal GitLab repositories. Read that sequence carefully, because it tells you three things that change the response. First, the cluster relationship is the lateral movement path: compromising the edge node gets you the internal nodes, because they trust each other and share the same compiled-in cookie. Second, the objective was not the video platform - it was a foothold from which to enumerate Windows infrastructure. Third, and most damaging, credentials in internal GitLab repositories were the prize. If you patch Expressway and do nothing else, and your GitLab repositories contain service account passwords, API keys or connection strings, you have closed the door and left the keys outside.

Public exploit code exists, and this matters for the timeline. Multiple aggregators list proof-of-concept exploits for CVE-2026-76466, described as unauthenticated remote RCE via hard-coded credentials in the cluster database service. One report characterises the exploitation as having followed soon after the public PoC dropped. The combination of a compiled-in universal credential, a network-reachable Erlang port, public exploit code and no workaround is about as unfavourable as a vulnerability gets.

Why this lands hard on UK government. Cisco Expressway and VCS are the standard Cisco edge for Mobile and Remote Access and business-to-business video, and they are widely deployed across NHS trusts, local authorities, central government departments and universities - frequently with Expressway-E deliberately internet-facing, because that is its job. The architecture that makes Expressway useful is the architecture this vulnerability exploits. The single highest-value action, if you cannot patch before Monday, is blocking TCP 4372 at the boundary: because the credential is universal and unchangeable, port reachability is effectively the entire exposure.

Confidence and caveats. High on the CVE identifier, the 9.8 score, the CWE-798 classification, the Erlang cluster database service on TCP 4372, the universal compiled-in cookie, root-level impact, the X15.5.20 fixed release, the absence of a workaround, the clustered-only scope, the 20 November KEV addition and the 23 November deadline. Medium on the intrusion chain detail - the two-edge-nodes-then-two-internal-nodes sequence, the Python scanning scripts and the GitLab credential theft come from secondary reporting rather than a named incident response publication, and no victim or actor has been named. One source raises a mapping concern: it states that the Cisco advisory text it retrieved does not mention CVE-2026-76466, and suggests the advisory and the CVE may be distinct issues that one upgrade happens to address. This feed could not verify that against cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t directly - all page fetches failed on DNS resolution. Check the Cisco advisory before you rely on the CVE-to-advisory mapping in your change record.
recommended_actions: Block TCP 4372 at the network boundary today, before you do anything else. The Erlang cookie is compiled into the software and identical on every install, so there is no credential to rotate and reachability is the entire exposure. This is the single highest-value action in this entry and it does not require a maintenance window.

Upgrade clustered Expressway-C and Expressway-E to X15.5.20. CISA's deadline is Monday 23 November. There is no workaround, so the only alternatives to upgrading are blocking the port and accepting the risk in writing.

Confirm whether your deployment is actually clustered before you schedule emergency downtime on a video platform. Non-clustered deployments are reported as unaffected, and unnecessary emergency change on a clinical or public-facing video service carries its own risk.

Then act on the chain, not just the CVE: audit your internal GitLab, and any other internal source control, for credentials. The reported objective was pulling credentials from internal GitLab repositories. Patching Expressway does not remove secrets already committed to repositories, and if those secrets were taken, the intrusion continues without the vulnerability.

Rotate any credential that a compromised Expressway node could have reached, including anything recoverable from internal repositories. Prioritise service accounts, API keys and database connection strings over user passwords.

Hunt for the post-exploitation behaviour specifically: Python processes on or originating from Expressway nodes, SMB share enumeration, SQL Server and WinRM probing from the Expressway management segment. These are the signals that distinguish exploited from merely vulnerable.

Treat all cluster peers as compromised if any one node was reachable and unpatched. The reported chain moved from internet-facing nodes to internal cluster members, because they trust each other by design.

Verify the CVE-to-advisory mapping against Cisco advisory cisco-sa-vcs-static-cred-hr7EWZ8t before writing your change record. One source reports the advisory text it retrieved does not name CVE-2026-76466; this feed could not confirm either way.

Review why Expressway-E was reachable on 4372 from the internet at all. The service is for cluster replication, not for clients. If your boundary policy allowed it, assume other management ports are similarly exposed and scan from outside to find out.

kql.name: Inbound connections to Expressway cluster database port TCP 4372
kql.description: Primary detection. Any connection to 4372 from outside the cluster replication path is an exploitation attempt against a universal compiled-in credential. External-source hits should be treated as incidents, not findings.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
let clusterPeers = dynamic([]);  // populate with your Expressway cluster node IPs
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort == 4372
| extend PeerKnown = iff(array_length(clusterPeers) > 0 and SourceIP in (clusterPeers), true, false)
| where PeerKnown == false
| summarize Attempts = count(), Targets = make_set(DestinationIP, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated), Actions = make_set(DeviceAction, 5)
    by SourceIP, SourceIsExternal = not(ipv4_is_private(SourceIP))
| order by SourceIsExternal desc, Attempts desc

kql.name: Expressway root-level command execution and unexpected process activity
kql.description: Exploitation yields command execution as root on the Expressway OS. Surfaces shell, interpreter and privilege indicators in Expressway appliance syslog. Requires Expressway syslog forwarding to Sentinel.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where Computer has_any ("expressway", "expwy", "vcs-", "vcse", "vcsc")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/sh", "/bin/bash", "python", "perl", "root shell", "erlang", "erl_call", "epmd", "cookie", "COMMAND=", "sudo:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Lateral movement from Expressway nodes - SMB, SQL Server and WinRM probing
kql.description: Post-exploitation detection matching the reported chain: custom Python scripts scanning for SMB shares and probing SQL Server and WinRM. Replace the expresswayNodes list with your actual node addresses.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
let expresswayNodes = dynamic([]);  // populate with your Expressway node IPs
let targetPorts = dynamic([445, 139, 1433, 1434, 5985, 5986, 3389]);
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where array_length(expresswayNodes) == 0 or SourceIP in (expresswayNodes)
| where DestinationPort in (targetPorts)
| summarize DistinctTargets = dcount(DestinationIP), DistinctPorts = dcount(DestinationPort), Attempts = count(), PortList = make_set(DestinationPort, 10)
    by SourceIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctTargets >= 5 or DistinctPorts >= 3
| order by DistinctTargets desc

kql.name: Anomalous access to internal GitLab and source control repositories
kql.description: The reported objective was pulling credentials from internal GitLab repositories. Surfaces repository access patterns consistent with bulk cloning or scraping rather than developer activity. Adapt the table to your GitLab logging source.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/gitlab", ".git/", "/api/v4/projects", "/raw/", "/archive", "repository/files")
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctPaths = dcount(csUriStem), Bytes = sum(scBytes), UA = make_set(csUserAgent, 5)
    by cIP, csUserName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where DistinctPaths > 25 or Requests > 200
| order by DistinctPaths desc

kql.name: Windows-side view of inbound enumeration from the video edge segment
kql.description: Catches the same lateral movement from the receiving end, for estates where Expressway appliances are not themselves logging to Sentinel. Surfaces Windows hosts receiving SMB, SQL and WinRM connections from unexpected internal sources.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
let targetPorts = dynamic([445, 1433, 5985, 5986]);
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType == "InboundConnectionAccepted"
| where LocalPort in (targetPorts)
| where RemoteIPType == "Private"
| summarize AcceptedConnections = count(), DistinctHosts = dcount(DeviceId), Ports = make_set(LocalPort, 5), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by RemoteIP
| where DistinctHosts >= 5
| order by DistinctHosts desc

kql.name: Python-based scanning tooling execution
kql.description: The reported chain used custom Python scripts for SMB, SQL Server and WinRM reconnaissance. Surfaces Python execution with networking or enumeration arguments on servers that have no reason to run it.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName has_any ("python", "python3", "python.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("smbclient", "impacket", "socket", "connect(", "445", "1433", "5985", "winrm", "smb", "gitlab", "clone")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

vulnerabilities.title: NHS England Digital Alerts CC-4898 and CC-4900, and the Outlook Zero-Day CVE-2026-124194 Whose KEV Deadline Is Tuesday 24 November - Patched Through the Office Updater, Not Windows Update, So Your Patch Compliance Dashboard Will Report Green
affected_products: Microsoft Outlook - CVE-2026-124194, spoofing / NTLMv2 hash disclosure, actively exploited
Microsoft November 2026 Patch Tuesday (10 November) - reported variously as 1,093, 1,094 or 1,235 CVEs; 63 rated critical
PHP 8.6 - fixed in 8.6.0 (NHS England alert CC-4900)
PHP 8.5 - fixed in 8.5.13
PHP 8.4 - fixed in 8.4.28
PHP 8.3 - fixed in 8.3.37
PHP 8.2 - fixed in 8.2.36
Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938 - carried in NHS England alert of 18 November
vulnerabilities.summary:
This entry exists because of a delivery mechanism, not a severity score. CVE-2026-124194 is a Microsoft Outlook spoofing vulnerability rated only CVSS 6.5, which under most organisations' triage rules would be a routine monthly patch. It is being actively exploited, CISA has added it to the KEV catalogue with a federal remediation deadline of Tuesday 24 November 2026, and NHS England's National CSOC rates future exploitation as highly likely in cyber alert CC-4898. The trap is that the fix ships through Office's own update channel rather than Windows Update. If your patch compliance reporting is built on WSUS, Intune Windows update rings or SCCM software update compliance, it will show this estate as fully patched while every Outlook client remains vulnerable. That mismatch is the entire reason this is at rank 4 rather than rank 10.

The mechanism, and why 6.5 understates it. An unauthenticated attacker sends a specially crafted message file and induces the recipient to open it in Outlook. Outlook then connects to an attacker-controlled network location without presenting the usual external-content warning, and in doing so discloses the user's NTLMv2 authentication hash. The CVSS score reflects the user interaction requirement and the limited direct impact. What it does not reflect is what an NTLMv2 hash is worth in a UK public sector estate: it is relay material and offline cracking material, and in environments where SMB signing is incomplete or NTLM has not been disabled - which describes a great many NHS trusts and local authorities - a leaked hash is a path to authenticated access rather than an information disclosure. The absence of the external-content warning is the part that defeats user training: the standard advice to be suspicious of prompts does not help when there is no prompt.

Microsoft has published no detail on the attacks and has not identified the actor. The total CVE count for November's Patch Tuesday is reported inconsistently across outlets - 1,093 in several, 1,094 in one, 1,235 in others, with 63 critical - and NHS England's CC-4898 cites 1,235. The discrepancy is almost certainly a counting convention (Microsoft-issued CVEs versus all CVEs addressed including third-party components such as Chromium), and it does not affect the action. One zero-day, actively exploited, deadline Tuesday.

The NHS alerts, which are the UK government hook. NHS England Digital published CC-4898 on 19 November covering the Microsoft November updates, explicitly noting CISA's KEV addition of CVE-2026-124194 and rating future exploitation highly likely. On the same day it published CC-4900 covering seven critical PHP vulnerabilities, rated Medium, with the National CSOC stating it is aware of public proof-of-concept exploits and assessing future exploitation as a realistic possibility; fixed versions are 8.6.0, 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36. These sit alongside CC-4899 (vCenter, rank 1) and the 18 November Java4Shell alert for CVE-2026-114938, where the CSOC rates future exploitation as likely and notes unauthenticated remote code execution is possible. That is four cyber alerts in two days, three of them concerning actively exploited or imminently exploitable flaws. Note also a sourcing discrepancy worth resolving locally: the Microsoft alert surfaced in search under both CC-4889 and CC-4898, so match on content rather than identifier when you reconcile your queue.

The PHP item deserves a specific comment for the public sector. Seven critical vulnerabilities with public PoC code, across a language that underpins an enormous volume of UK local authority and NHS trust web estate - much of it on legacy branches, much of it managed by third parties under contracts that do not specify patch windows. The 8.2 and 8.3 fixed versions in that list are the ones to worry about, because an organisation still running 8.2 in November 2026 is unlikely to have a mature update pipeline.

Confidence and caveats. High on CVE-2026-124194 as an actively exploited Outlook spoofing flaw, the CVSS 6.5 score, the NTLMv2 hash disclosure mechanism, the suppressed external-content warning, the KEV listing with a 24 November deadline, the Office-updater delivery path, the existence and substance of CC-4898, CC-4900 and the Java4Shell alert, and the PHP fixed version numbers. Medium on the exact Patch Tuesday CVE total, which sources contradict, and on the CC-4889/CC-4898 identifier. No attribution exists. No IOCs have been published for the Outlook exploitation, so the detections below are behavioural - outbound SMB and WebDAV from Outlook, and NTLM authentication to unexpected destinations. All direct page fetches failed in this run; NHS alert content is from search-surfaced summaries of digital.nhs.uk pages rather than the pages themselves.
recommended_actions: Before Tuesday: verify Outlook client patch state through the Office update channel, not through Windows Update compliance. This is the action most likely to be skipped, because your existing dashboard will already say you are compliant. Pull Office build numbers directly.

Fix the reporting gap permanently, not just for this CVE. If your patch compliance posture cannot distinguish 'Windows is patched' from 'Office is patched', you have a structural blind spot that will recur every time Microsoft ships an Office-channel security fix. Add Office build reporting to the same dashboard your board sees.

Block outbound SMB (TCP 445) and WebDAV to the internet at the perimeter if you have not already. This breaks the exploitation path for hash disclosure regardless of client patch state and is the strongest compensating control available.

Audit NTLM usage and enforce SMB signing. A leaked NTLMv2 hash is relay and cracking material; in an estate with incomplete SMB signing it converts to authenticated access. If you have been deferring NTLM reduction, this is the business case.

Do not rely on user awareness for this one. Outlook connects to the attacker location without the usual external-content warning, so the standard 'be suspicious of prompts' training has nothing to act on.

NHS organisations: reconcile CC-4898, CC-4899, CC-4900 and the 18 November Java4Shell alert as a single batch rather than working them in date order. Three of the four concern actively exploited or PoC-available flaws, and two carry deadlines inside 48 hours. Match the Microsoft alert on content - it has surfaced under both CC-4889 and CC-4898.

Patch PHP to 8.6.0, 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 or 8.2.36 per branch. Public PoC code exists for seven critical vulnerabilities. Prioritise internet-facing estate and anything on the 8.2 or 8.3 branches, where update pipelines are typically weakest.

Inventory which parts of your PHP web estate are managed by third parties and whether those contracts specify a patch window. For most UK local authorities the answer is 'several' and 'no', and that is the finding, not the patching.
Address Java4Shell CVE-2026-114938 if it remains open from the 18 November alert - unauthenticated remote code execution, with the NHS CSOC rating future exploitation as likely.

kql.name: Outlook initiating outbound SMB or WebDAV - CVE-2026-124194 hash disclosure
kql.description: Primary detection. Exploitation induces Outlook to connect to an attacker-controlled network location, leaking the NTLMv2 hash. Outlook has no legitimate reason to make outbound SMB connections to public addresses.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("outlook.exe", "olk.exe")
| where RemotePort in (445, 139, 80, 443)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public"
| where ActionType in ("ConnectionSuccess", "ConnectionAttempt")
| summarize Connections = count(), Ports = make_set(RemotePort, 5), Urls = make_set(RemoteUrl, 10), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp), LastSeen = max(Timestamp)
    by DeviceName, AccountName = InitiatingProcessAccountName, RemoteIP
| where Ports has_any (445, 139) or Connections > 5
| order by LastSeen desc

kql.name: NTLM authentication attempts to external or unexpected destinations
kql.description: Catches the consequence rather than the cause - NTLM credential material leaving the estate. Surfaces NTLM authentication events with external or unrecognised targets following suspected exploitation.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where ActionType has_any ("NtlmAuthentication", "SmbSessionSetup", "LdapSearch")
| extend Target = tostring(parse_json(AdditionalFields).TargetServerName)
| where isnotempty(Target)
| where Target !endswith ".local" and Target !endswith "corp" and Target !has "internal"
| summarize Attempts = count(), Devices = dcount(DeviceId), Accounts = make_set(AccountName, 10)
    by Target, ActionType
| order by Attempts desc

kql.name: Crafted message-file attachments delivered to mailboxes
kql.description: Exploitation requires the victim to open a specially crafted message file. Surfaces .msg, .eml, .oft and .ics attachments arriving from external senders, so you can scope who was targeted even without published IOCs.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
EmailAttachmentInfo
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName endswith ".msg" or FileName endswith ".eml" or FileName endswith ".oft" or FileName endswith ".ics"
| join kind=inner (EmailEvents | where Timestamp > ago(lookback) | where EmailDirection == "Inbound") on NetworkMessageId
| project Timestamp, SenderFromAddress, RecipientEmailAddress, Subject, FileName, FileType, SHA256, DeliveryAction, ThreatTypes
| order by Timestamp desc

kql.name: Office and Outlook build inventory - the Windows Update blind spot
kql.description: The compliance query that matters for this entry. Reports Office/Outlook versions from software inventory rather than Windows update state, because CVE-2026-124194 ships through the Office updater and will not appear in Windows patch compliance.
kql.query:
let lookback = 7d;
DeviceTvmSoftwareInventory
| where SoftwareVendor has "microsoft"
| where SoftwareName has_any ("office", "outlook", "365 apps")
| summarize Devices = dcount(DeviceId), DeviceList = make_set(DeviceName, 25)
    by SoftwareName, SoftwareVersion
| order by SoftwareName asc, SoftwareVersion asc

kql.name: Outbound SMB to the internet at the perimeter
kql.description: Compensating control verification. Confirms whether outbound TCP 445 and 139 are actually blocked at the boundary, which breaks the hash disclosure path regardless of client patch state. Verify by evidence, not by reading the firewall policy.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
CommonSecurityLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where DestinationPort in (445, 139)
| where not(ipv4_is_private(DestinationIP))
| summarize Attempts = count(), Allowed = countif(DeviceAction !has "deny" and DeviceAction !has "block" and DeviceAction !has "drop"), Sources = dcount(SourceIP), Destinations = make_set(DestinationIP, 20)
    by bin(TimeGenerated, 1d)
| extend Verdict = iff(Allowed > 0, "EGRESS PERMITTED - remediate", "blocked")
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: PHP version inventory against NHS England CC-4900 fixed releases
kql.description: Supports CC-4900. Extracts PHP version strings from web server logs and flags anything below the fixed releases 8.6.0, 8.5.13, 8.4.28, 8.3.37 and 8.2.36, where seven critical vulnerabilities with public PoC code are unpatched.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has "PHP"
| extend PhpVersion = extract(@"PHP/?\s?(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(PhpVersion)
| extend Branch = strcat(split(PhpVersion, ".")[0], ".", split(PhpVersion, ".")[1])
| summarize Hosts = make_set(Computer, 25), Sightings = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by PhpVersion, Branch
| extend FixedForBranch = case(Branch == "8.6", "8.6.0", Branch == "8.5", "8.5.13", Branch == "8.4", "8.4.28", Branch == "8.3", "8.3.37", Branch == "8.2", "8.2.36", "unsupported-branch-upgrade-required")
| order by Branch asc, PhpVersion asc

vulnerabilities.title: Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448: The Mitigation Most Administrators Applied Does Not Work, the Affected Range Is Far Wider Than First Reported (4.0.0 Onward, Not Just 6.1.5), and CISA's Own Enrichment Record Contradicts Its KEV Listing
affected_products: Apache Roller 4.0.0 through 6.1.4 - per the CVE record
Apache Roller 6.1.5 - covered by the earlier duplicate identifier CVE-2026-82384; treat 4.0.0 through 6.1.5 as vulnerable
Fixed: 6.1.6; 6.1.7 released 11 November 2026 with 15 further CVE fixes and is the recommended target
Vulnerable component: XML-RPC servlet at /roller-services/xmlrpc with vendor extension types enabled
CWE-502 - deserialisation of untrusted data, pre-authentication
vulnerabilities.summary:
Carried from yesterday's rank 3 and given its own entry, because the window has materially widened the problem and because this remains the most dangerous false assurance in this report. Three things changed.

First, the affected range is much wider than originally reported. Yesterday this feed recorded the September fix under CVE-2026-82384 as covering 6.1.5 only. The CVE record for CVE-2026-129448 covers versions 4.0.0 through 6.1.4, and CVE-2026-129448 is a duplicate of CVE-2026-82384. Taken together, the correct working assumption is that every Roller install from 4.0.0 through 6.1.5 is vulnerable. That is an eighteen-year version range. Any UK organisation that checked its Roller estate against '6.1.5' and concluded it was unaffected has reached the wrong answer, and organisations running genuinely old Roller instances - which, for a blogging platform, frequently means a forgotten departmental or project site rather than a managed service - are the most exposed and the least likely to be looking.

Second, the mitigation that most administrators will have applied does not work. Disabling XML-RPC through the Roller admin interface does NOT mitigate this, because affected versions process and deserialise the request before checking whether the feature is enabled. The mitigations that do work are: set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping entirely, then restart Roller. Blocking the path at a proxy or WAF also works unless desktop blogging clients legitimately need it. This is the item in this report most likely to have produced a closed ticket over an open vulnerability.

Third, 6.1.6 is not the end state. Roller 6.1.7 was released on 11 November 2026 with fifteen further CVE fixes. If you are patching this weekend, go to 6.1.7, not 6.1.6 - otherwise you will be back in the same change queue within weeks.

The evidence problem, stated plainly because it affects how much weight you should give the KEV deadline. Apache published the CVE on 17 November 2026 stating the issue is being actively exploited, without sharing compromise details or payloads. CISA added it to KEV on 20 November with a 23 November deadline. But CISA's own enrichment record for the CVE, dated 18 November, shows the SSVC exploitation field as 'none', and at least one source states the CVE does not appear in the KEV catalogue at all. Those statements cannot all be true simultaneously. The most probable reconciliation is that the enrichment record predates the KEV decision and was not refreshed, and that the source reporting no KEV listing checked before the 20 November batch - but this feed cannot verify that, because every direct page fetch failed on DNS resolution in this run. The operational answer is unaffected: a pre-authentication deserialisation RCE in a web-facing Java application with a public proof-of-concept is worth patching this weekend regardless of which evidence field CISA has populated. But if you are asked to justify an emergency change on the strength of the KEV listing, know that the underlying evidence trail is inconsistent.

A detail about the PoC timeline that should change how you think about disclosure. Public proof-of-concept exploit code has existed on GitHub since approximately 28 September 2026 - roughly seven weeks before Apache published the advisory on 17 November. The exploitation Apache reports was therefore almost certainly occurring during a period when defenders had no advisory to act on, while attackers had working code. There is nothing to do about that retrospectively, but it is the argument for why an organisation's exposure management cannot rest solely on vendor advisories and KEV listings.

UK relevance. Roller is not a major UK government platform in the way vCenter or Expressway are, and no UK victim has been reported. Its relevance is structural: an unauthenticated, pre-authentication deserialisation RCE reaching back to 4.0.0, in a self-hosted Java web application, is exactly the profile of the forgotten internet-facing service that sits outside a UK public sector organisation's managed estate and outside its vulnerability scanning scope. Find it by scanning for the endpoint, not by querying your asset register.

Confidence and caveats. Medium overall, driven down by the evidence contradiction. High on the CWE-502 classification, the mechanism, the ineffective admin-UI mitigation, the working mitigations, the 6.1.7 release of 11 November and the duplicate relationship with CVE-2026-82384. Medium on the exact affected range, where sources conflict - one states the fix landed in 6.1.5, which contradicts the CVE record; verify against Apache's advisory. Low on exploitation evidence quality: Apache asserts active exploitation but publishes nothing, CISA's SSVC field says otherwise, and no victim, actor or payload has been named anywhere.
recommended_actions: First, undo the mitigation you probably applied. If you disabled XML-RPC through the Roller admin interface and closed the ticket, you are still vulnerable - affected versions deserialise the request before checking the feature flag. Reopen it.

Apply a mitigation that actually works: set enabledForExtensions to false in WEB-INF/web.xml, or remove the /roller-services/xmlrpc servlet mapping, then restart Roller. Blocking POST requests to /roller-services/xmlrpc at the proxy or WAF also works, unless desktop blogging clients genuinely need it.
Upgrade to 6.1.7, not 6.1.6. 6.1.7 shipped on 11 November with fifteen further CVE fixes; stopping at 6.1.6 puts you back in the change queue within weeks.

Re-scope your Roller inventory against 4.0.0 through 6.1.5, not against 6.1.5 alone. The CVE record covers 4.0.0 onward. If you checked only for 6.1.5 you have the wrong answer, and old forgotten instances are the most exposed.

Specifically re-check anything you patched in September under CVE-2026-82384. That release addressed 6.1.5 only, and CVE-2026-129448 is the same bug with a far wider range - a closed September ticket is not evidence that this is closed.

Find Roller by scanning for the /roller-services/xmlrpc endpoint across your external estate rather than by querying your asset register. A forgotten departmental blog is both the likeliest instance and the one your CMDB does not know about.

Do not let the evidence contradiction stall the change. CISA's enrichment record dated 18 November shows SSVC exploitation 'none' while KEV lists it with a 23 November deadline, and one source reports no KEV listing at all. A pre-auth deserialisation RCE with a seven-week-old public PoC justifies the patch on its own merits.

If a vulnerable instance was internet-facing at any point since late September, hunt rather than just patch. Public PoC code has existed since around 28 September, seven weeks before the advisory - the exposure window predates the disclosure.

Verify the affected range and fixed version against Apache's own advisory before finalising your change record. One source states the fix landed in 6.1.5, which contradicts the CVE record, and this run could not retrieve the advisory directly.

kql.name: POST requests to the Roller XML-RPC endpoint
kql.description: Primary detection. Any POST to /roller-services/xmlrpc from an unexpected source is an exploitation attempt, because affected versions deserialise before checking the feature flag. Lookback extends past the late-September PoC publication.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has "xmlrpc" or csUriStem has "roller-services"
| where csMethod == "POST"
| summarize Requests = count(), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), UserAgents = make_set(csUserAgent, 10), BytesIn = sum(csBytes), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by cIP, csUriStem, sSiteName
| extend External = not(ipv4_is_private(cIP))
| order by External desc, Requests desc

kql.name: Java deserialisation payload markers in request bodies and query strings
kql.description: Hunts the serialised Java object signature. Base64-encoded Java serialisation begins rO0AB; gadget chain class names also appear in some payloads. Requires request body or query string logging to be enabled.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriQuery has_any ("rO0AB", "java.lang.Runtime", "javax.management", "org.apache.commons.collections", "InvokerTransformer", "BadAttributeValueExpException", "ysoserial")
    or csUriStem has "xmlrpc"
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Child process execution from a Java application server - post-deserialisation RCE
kql.description: Catches the consequence of successful deserialisation. A Tomcat, Jetty or java process spawning a shell or network utility is the strongest evidence of exploitation available without the payload itself.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("tomcat", "catalina", "jetty", "java", "roller")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("/bin/sh", "/bin/bash", "curl", "wget", "nc ", "ncat", "python", "perl", "base64 -d", "chmod +x", "/tmp/")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Facility, SeverityLevel, SyslogMessage
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: Discover forgotten Roller instances across the estate
kql.description: Inventory query. Roller's exposure profile is the forgotten departmental blog that is not in the CMDB. Surfaces any site serving Roller paths so you can scope the real estate rather than the recorded one.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/roller", "roller-services", "/roller-ui", "weblog", "rsd.jsp", "/apache-roller")
| summarize Requests = count(), Paths = make_set(csUriStem, 20), DistinctClients = dcount(cIP), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by sSiteName, sComputerName, sIP
| order by Requests desc

kql.name: Web application server spawning interpreters or download tools
kql.description: Endpoint-side equivalent of the syslog query, for Roller instances hosted on EDR-covered servers. Java spawning shells, interpreters or download utilities indicates successful deserialisation RCE.
kql.query:
let lookback = 90d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("java", "java.exe", "tomcat.exe", "catalina.sh", "jsvc")
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "cmd.exe", "powershell.exe", "curl", "wget", "python", "python3", "perl", "nc", "ncat", "certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc

vulnerabilities.title: The UK Publicly Confirms Offensive Cyber Operations Against Russia, China, Iran and North Korea - and the Retaliation Risk Lands on Operators, Not on Government: NCSC Recorded 1,831 Attacks With 80 Nationally Significant, MI5 Links 50+ Arrests to Iran
vulnerabilities.vendor: UK Ministry of Defence / National Cyber Force / NCSC
affected_products: UK critical national infrastructure operators - energy, water, transport, health, telecommunications
UK central government departments and agencies
UK defence supply chain
National Cyber Force - new headquarters at Samlesbury, Lancashire
Cyber and Specialist Operations Command
vulnerabilities.summary:
This broke on 20 November and propagated through the window, with international coverage dated 21 November, so it belongs in this report as the strategic UK government item. General Sir Rob Magowan, head of the military's Cyber and Specialist Operations Command, told Sky News that Britain conducts offensive cyber operations against Iran, Russia, China and North Korea. Asked directly whether the National Cyber Force runs offensive operations, he answered 'Absolutely, and we've been clear about that.' He said the force can map an adversary's networks and act within them, and that operations are succeeding. He also said: 'I wouldn't say we're at war, but we're not at peace either.' The interview coincided with the opening of the force's new headquarters at Samlesbury, Lancashire, officially opened by King Charles III. Coverage also indicates the force targets organised crime groups and individuals causing online harm, including harm to children.

Why a ministerial-level disclosure belongs in a threat intelligence feed rather than a policy digest. Because the consequence of a state publicly confirming offensive operations against four adversaries does not fall on that state's military networks, which are defended accordingly. It falls on the operators - the energy companies, water utilities, hospital trusts, transport authorities and their suppliers - because those are the accessible targets when a hostile state wants to respond to the UK without engaging the UK's military. The practical reading for a UK CNI operator is not that an attack is imminent; it is that the political temperature has been publicly raised, and the organisations that absorb that are the ones in this report's other entries.

The numbers published alongside it give the base rate. The NCSC tracked 1,831 reported cyber attacks in the past year, of which 80 were nationally significant. That ratio - roughly one in twenty-three reported incidents reaching national significance - is the most useful single figure in this entry for anyone sizing an incident response capability. MI5 has linked more than 50 arrests in Britain in the past year to Iran-linked operations, which indicates the Iranian threat to the UK is substantially a physical-proximity and recruitment problem as well as a network one.

The Iranian precedent is the part that makes this concrete, and it is worth restating because it is the only documented case of disruptive state attack on UK critical infrastructure. In July 2026, hackers reported as linked to Iran's IRGC shut down a small UK power station, which was offline for four days while staff worked to restore control. The Telegraph and Financial Times reported it in August. It is believed to be the first disruptive Iranian cyberattack of its kind in the UK. The Government has never formally attributed it to Iran or to any government or group, and a Government spokesperson stated that 'at no point was there a risk to the wider energy system'. The plant has not been named. The attack reportedly coincided with Iranian-linked intrusions into US water utilities across twelve states. Note the shape of that incident: a small asset, four days of lost control, no formal attribution, and no public technical detail. That is the model UK operators should plan against - not a spectacular national outage, but a modest operational technology asset losing control for days, with no authoritative post-incident report to learn from.

How this connects to the rest of the report. The NCSC's annual report of 3 November judged that AI-enabled malware is highly likely to be used in a ransomware attack on UK critical national infrastructure, possibly within two years, and that criminals will very probably deploy AI-driven malware against Britain's essential services by 2028. In this report, rank 1 is a PRC-nexus actor with ten weeks of undetected access to virtualisation management planes, rank 8 records a ransomware group that has spent over $7,000 on generative AI services to build its own reconnaissance tooling, and the 3AM intrusion against a UK school estate in September showed suspected AI-assisted operation. The NCSC's two-year horizon is being tested now.

Confidence and caveats. High confidence that the statements were made and the headquarters opened - this is on-record, widely reported, and attributed to a named officer. Nothing about the operations themselves is verifiable: the Government has released no operational detail and the reporting rests on a single on-record interview. The NCSC figures of 1,831 and 80 are as reported in coverage of that interview and should be checked against the NCSC Annual Review itself before quoting to a board. The Iranian power station attack remains media-reported and formally unattributed; the July-versus-August timing differs between outlets because the attack and its reporting were in different months. One source in this run also referenced an Autumn Budget 2026 figure of nearly two hundred billion pounds for AI-driven government cybersecurity projects - this feed considers that figure implausible on its face, the same article reportedly contained an apparent error, and it is recorded here only so that nobody repeats it without checking.
recommended_actions: Brief your board on the shift in posture rather than on the headline. The operative change is that the UK has publicly confirmed offensive operations against four hostile states, and the retaliatory surface for those states is commercial and public sector operators, not the MoD.

Use the one-in-twenty-three ratio - 80 nationally significant incidents out of 1,831 reported to the NCSC in a year - as the planning base rate when you are asked whether your incident response capability is proportionate.

Plan against the shape of the July power station incident, not against a national outage: a modest OT asset losing operator control for days, no formal attribution, no public technical detail, and therefore no external playbook. Ask specifically how long you could run a given plant or site on manual control.

If you operate OT or industrial control systems, test the control-restoration path rather than the detection path. The documented UK incident was four days to restore control, which is a recovery problem, not a detection problem.

For Iran specifically, treat insider and physical-proximity risk as co-equal with network risk. MI5 links more than 50 arrests in Britain in the past year to Iran-linked operations, which is a recruitment and access pattern, not an exploitation one.

Confirm you can actually reach the NCSC and your sector regulator out of hours, and that someone other than the CISO knows how. Nationally significant incidents are handled on relationships established in advance.

Re-test the assumption that your OT estate is air-gapped. The RDM refrigeration operation in this feed's recent runs found thousands of UK devices internet-reachable that their operators believed were not, and the NCSC's remedy there was explicit: patch, change default credentials, get them off the internet.

Do not quote the NCSC's 1,831 and 80 figures, or the reported Autumn Budget cyber funding figure, without checking them against the NCSC Annual Review and HM Treasury documents respectively. The budget figure in particular appeared in a source this feed assesses as unreliable.
