vulnerabilities.title: Transport for London Oyster Photocard Breach Holds at Around 265,000 Customers With No New Information in the Window - the Portal Remains Offline and the Intrusion Route Is Still Undisclosed Six Days On
affected_products: TfL Oyster photocard online portal - taken offline 16 November 2026, still offline
Zip Oyster photocard accounts (under-18s)
18+ Student Oyster photocard accounts
18-25 Care Leaver Oyster photocard accounts
60+ London Oyster photocard accounts
Apprentice Oyster photocard accounts
Veterans Oyster photocard accounts
vulnerabilities.summary:
Demoted from rank 2 to rank 7, and the reason is stated plainly: there was no new information in this window. The most recent substantive coverage remains 19 November. This entry is retained rather than rotated out because it is the live UK government incident in this report - TfL is a statutory body under the Greater London Authority - the portal is still offline, and the remediation step that affects customers has not yet happened.

What is established. TfL detected the incident on 16 November 2026 and took the Oyster photocard system offline to limit access. Around 265,000 Oyster photocard customers may have had account details exposed, revised up from an initial 250,000 figure, with some outlets reporting 'over 260,000'. The exposed data comprises email addresses, phone numbers, home addresses, dates of birth, and security questions and answers. TfL states that passwords, bank and payment card details, journey history and photocard photographs were not compromised, and that names and dates of birth on Zip Oyster cards for children were not compromised. Cards continue to work. Once the portal is restored, all photocard customers will be prompted to change their password, security question and answer.

The part that has not improved and should be pressed. TfL has not said how the attackers got in. Six days after detection, with a revised-upward victim count and a system still offline, the absence of any statement on initial access is the most significant open question. It matters beyond TfL: other UK public bodies cannot check whether they share the weakness. If the route was credential stuffing against the portal - which the compromise of individual customer accounts, with no indication of a backend database theft, would be consistent with - then every UK public sector customer portal with the same authentication design is exposed to the same technique, and the lesson is available immediately. If it was an application vulnerability or a supplier compromise, the lesson is different. Nobody outside TfL can act on either, because TfL has not said. That is the criticism to make.

Why the security questions and answers remain the defining problem. This feed has said it on each previous run and it stays true: of everything exposed, security question answers are the one category that cannot be rotated. A mother's maiden name, a first school, a first pet - these are fixed facts about a person's life, reused across banking, utilities, telecoms and government services. TfL prompting customers to change their security question and answer on the restored portal protects the TfL account; it does nothing about the same answer sitting in a bank's identity verification process. Combined with home addresses and dates of birth for a population that includes children on Zip cards, over-60s and care leavers, this is a dataset built for identity fraud and for targeted social engineering against groups with elevated vulnerability.

The second-breach framing is also worth keeping in view. This follows TfL's 2024 cyberattack, which affected customer services. Two significant incidents at the same transport authority inside roughly two years is a pattern that a board, the GLA and the London Assembly should be asking about, independent of the technical specifics of either.

Confidence and caveats. High on the detection date, the system being taken offline, the approximate 265,000 figure and its upward revision, the exposed and not-exposed data categories, the affected photocard types, cards continuing to work, and the planned credential reset on restoration. The exact count differs between outlets, with some reporting 'over 260,000', and TfL has indicated the investigation is incomplete and the figure may rise further - so treat 265,000 as a floor rather than a final number. No attribution, no threat actor claim, no ransomware leak site listing and no extortion demand have been reported. No initial access vector has been disclosed. The credential-stuffing hypothesis above is this feed's analytical inference from the reported facts and is explicitly not a sourced claim. No direct page fetch succeeded in this run.
recommended_actions: UK public bodies operating customer-facing portals: do not wait for TfL to publish a root cause. Assume credential stuffing against a portal with security-question-based recovery is viable against you and test it. That test is available today; TfL's root cause may never be.

Remove security questions and answers from account recovery flows wherever you still use them. They are unrotatable secrets, they are exposed in this breach for 265,000 people, and they are a weak second factor at best. Replace with email or SMS verification plus rate limiting, or with a proper second factor.

If you hold security question answers in a database, review why, and whether they are hashed. Many systems store them in plaintext or reversibly encrypted so that call-centre staff can read them aloud - which is also the reason they leak.
Enforce rate limiting and credential stuffing protection on every public authentication endpoint, and verify by testing against the endpoint rather than by reading the configuration.

Councils, NHS trusts and other bodies serving children, older people and care leavers: note the population in this breach. Fraud and social engineering against these groups is more likely to succeed, and your communications about any incident should be written for them rather than for a general audience.

If you are a TfL photocard holder or advising staff who are: change the same security question answer anywhere else it is used, particularly with banks and telecoms providers, rather than only on the restored TfL portal. The exposed answer is a fact about your life, not a password.

Watch for phishing that uses the exposed data to establish credibility - correct home address, correct date of birth, correct phone number - in messages about Oyster refunds, card replacements or account verification. The data set supports highly convincing approaches.

For boards: ask about incident repetition rather than incident detail. Two significant incidents at the same transport authority inside roughly two years is the governance question, and it is the same question your own organisation should be able to answer.

kql.name: Credential stuffing against public authentication endpoints
kql.description: Tests the hypothesis you can act on while TfL's root cause remains undisclosed. Surfaces high-volume authentication attempts with elevated failure rates against login endpoints - the signature of credential stuffing against a customer portal.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csMethod == "POST"
| where csUriStem has_any ("/login", "/signin", "/auth", "/account/logon", "/session", "/oauth/token")
| summarize Attempts = count(), Failures = countif(scStatus in (401, 403, 400)), Successes = countif(scStatus in (200, 302)), UAs = dcount(csUserAgent), Users = dcount(csUserName)
    by cIP, csUriStem, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| extend FailureRate = round(todouble(Failures) / todouble(Attempts), 2)
| where Attempts > 50 and FailureRate > 0.6
| order by Attempts desc

kql.name: Account recovery and security question endpoint abuse

| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("forgot", "reset", "recover", "security-question", "securityquestion", "challenge", "verify-identity")
| summarize Requests = count(), DistinctAccounts = dcount(csUserName), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), UAs = make_set(csUserAgent, 5)
    by cIP, csUriStem, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Requests > 20 or DistinctAccounts > 10
| order by Requests desc

AADSignInLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)

| order by IPs desc

kql.name: Bulk personal data egress from customer-facing applications
kql.description: Distinguishes mass data extraction from individual account compromise - the question TfL has not answered. Surfaces single clients retrieving unusually large volumes or unusually many distinct customer records.

let lookback = 45d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/account", "/profile", "/customer", "/api/user", "/details", "/export")
| summarize Requests = count(), TotalBytes = sum(scBytes), DistinctPaths = dcount(csUriStem), DistinctUsers = dcount(csUserName)
    by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Requests > 200 or TotalBytes > 50000000 or DistinctUsers > 50

| order by MBytes desc

vulnerabilities.title: UK Corporate and NHS Supply Chain Leak-Site Cluster: Halfords, Debenhams, Bensons for Beds, Boutinot, Waterman Group and NHS Dispensing Contractor Fittleworth - Low Confidence by Design, but N0n's Listings Describe a New Asset Class Nobody Has in Their Inventory: AI Storefront Assistant Data
vulnerabilities.vendor: Multiple UK corporates and NHS suppliers
affected_products: Halfords Group plc - LSE-listed automotive and cycling retailer - claimed by N0n, logged 20 November 2026
Debenhams - claimed by N0n
Bensons for Beds Retail Ltd - claimed by N0n, logged 16-17 November 2026
Company #239 - described as a UK fashion retailer - claimed by N0n, 18 November 2026
Company #157 - described as a UK bed retailer - claimed by N0n, 9 November 2026
Fittleworth Medical Ltd - NHS Dispensing Appliance Contractor - claimed by Scarlettgroup, logged 14 November, appeared in UK listings 20 November
Waterman Group - UK engineering consultancy - claimed by Rhysida, logged 16 November 2026
Boutinot Limited - UK wine importer - claimed by Aurora, 19 November 2026
SDJ Design Engineering - logged 20 November 2026
Simply UK - claimed by Qilin
Audio Note UK Ltd - claimed by Osiris, 11 November 2026
vulnerabilities.summary:
Confidence is low and that is deliberate. Every item here is a ransomware leak-site claim made by the attacker about itself. None has been confirmed by the named organisation, a regulator or an independent researcher, and one of the groups involved is documented as systematically fabricating victims. This entry exists for two reasons: the volume of UK listings in and around the window is worth recording, and one of the groups is describing a category of stolen data that most UK retailers do not have in their asset inventory at all.

Start with the reliability problem, because it governs everything below. Bitdefender's November 2026 Threat Debrief reports that analysis of data from N0n's own exposed file server indicates the group targeted just over 20 victims, while its leak site listed more than 100. Bitdefender removed 126 N0n entries from its October totals, revising the month from 1,072 to 946. Ransomware.live records N0n with around 190 to 260 listed victims depending on when you look, 116 in the last 30 days. The arithmetic is unavoidable: the large majority of N0n's listings are not real victims. Aurora and Rhysida listings have likewise been reported as including unverified or fabricated claims. So when you read that Halfords, Debenhams and Bensons for Beds have all been 'breached', the base rate says most of those claims are false - and Halfords' recent stock exchange announcements make no mention of a cyber incident, which for an LSE-listed company facing a material breach is meaningful negative evidence.

Now the part that is genuinely new and that survives the reliability problem. Look at what N0n says it took. From the Halfords listing: a semantic search index containing 189,280 'product meaning vectors', a directory of 54 staff and agency identities with storefront access, and an account map for UK, Ireland and .com storefronts. From the Bensons for Beds listing: shopper chat transcripts from a storefront assistant, thousands of customer messages, automated shopper profiling, and a product category intelligence map. Elsewhere in N0n's listings: a complete AI shopping assistant conversation corpus. These are not customer databases or finance systems. They are the artefacts of AI-powered retail: vector embeddings, conversation logs from chat assistants, and the service identities that connect them.

That matters whether or not these specific victims are real, and here is why. A vector index is a lossy but genuine representation of the corpus it was built from, and research has repeatedly shown embeddings can be partially inverted to recover source text. A chat assistant conversation corpus contains whatever customers typed into a box - which, in retail, routinely includes names, addresses, order numbers, payment problems and health information volunteered in the course of asking about a product. Almost no UK retailer's data protection impact assessment covers the vector store, and almost none of their asset registers list it. The listings may be fabricated; the exposure they describe is real and unmanaged across the sector. Note also that N0n is reported to have spent over $7,000 on generative AI services to develop scanning and reconnaissance scripts, and uses OpenCode to manage AI models - so a group that targets AI infrastructure is itself built on it.

The item that deserves separate attention is Fittleworth Medical, because it is not a retailer. Fittleworth is a UK national NHS Dispensing Appliance Contractor delivering stoma, continence and wound care supplies to patients' homes, and it receives prescriptions electronically through the NHS Electronic Prescription Service. Scarlettgroup listed fittleworth.com on 14 November, claiming to have encrypted sensitive data and stating it would publish in full if no contact was made. If that claim is true, the data concerns patients with stoma, continence and wound care needs - health information of a kind that is both special category under UK GDPR and acutely sensitive to the individuals concerned. There is no company statement, no regulator notice and no independent confirmation. It is listed at low confidence and flagged because the consequence if true is disproportionate to the probability, and because NHS England has separately announced it will investigate suppliers' security posture.

Waterman Group is the other item with asymmetric consequence. Rhysida listed this UK engineering consultancy on 16 November claiming roughly 205,000 files totalling about 784 GB, and one aggregator reports the claimed material includes a full password register covering Microsoft 365 and Azure, a Synology NAS, Dropbox administration and bank access. Waterman is an engineering consultancy that works on UK infrastructure projects. A claimed password register is the kind of artefact that converts one breach into several, and RedPacket explicitly notes the listing does not state that Waterman's systems were encrypted. No company statement exists.

Confidence and caveats. Low throughout, as stated. High confidence only that these listings exist on these leak sites on these dates, and that Bitdefender has documented N0n inflating its victim count by roughly a factor of five. No UK organisation named here has confirmed an incident. No ransom figures have been published. The Halfords post date conflicts between sources - 9 November in one report against a 20 November discovery date in the tracker - and such dates are frequently discovery rather than intrusion dates. The claimed data descriptions are the attackers' own words and should not be reported to a board as fact.
recommended_actions: Do not act on these listings as confirmed breaches, and do not let anyone brief them as such. Bitdefender's analysis of N0n's own file server indicates roughly 20 real victims against more than 100 listings. The base rate says most of these are false.

Do act on the asset class, because that is real regardless. Add your vector stores, embedding indexes and AI assistant conversation logs to your asset register and to your data protection impact assessments. Most UK retailers have neither, and N0n's listings describe exactly this material.

Specifically determine what your customer-facing chat assistant retains, for how long, and who can reach it. In retail, customers type names, addresses, order numbers, payment problems and sometimes health information into a product chat box. If that corpus is retained indefinitely and reachable by a storefront service account, it is an unmanaged special-category data store.

Treat a vector index as personal data, not as derived metadata. Embeddings are a lossy but genuine representation of their source corpus and research has shown they can be partially inverted to recover source text. A claim of 189,280 'product meaning vectors' is a claim about a real retrievable asset.

Audit storefront and e-commerce service identities. The Halfords listing claims a directory of 54 staff and agency identities with storefront access. Agency and contractor access to commerce platforms is routinely over-provisioned and under-reviewed, and that is a finding you can check today without reference to any leak site.

If you are named in any of these listings: check your own telemetry rather than responding to the listing, and specifically look for bulk retrieval from commerce APIs, vector database endpoints and chat transcript stores. Then decide on disclosure based on your evidence, not theirs.

NHS organisations and commissioners: seek assurance from Fittleworth Medical directly regarding the Scarlettgroup claim. The company is a national Dispensing Appliance Contractor receiving electronic prescriptions and handling stoma, continence and wound care data - special category data under UK GDPR. The claim is unverified; the consequence if true is disproportionate to the probability, which is precisely when assurance-seeking is warranted.

UK infrastructure clients of Waterman Group: note the claimed password register covering Microsoft 365, Azure, Synology NAS, Dropbox administration and bank access. If true, this is a breach that propagates. Ask whether credentials relating to your projects were held, and rotate any shared or federated access on the assumption they may have been.

For every supplier named here, use the claim as a prompt to check what access that supplier holds into your estate - which is useful whether or not the claim is true, and is the work the CSRB's designated critical supplier regime at rank 2 will eventually require anyway.

Record in your intelligence notes that N0n has invested over $7,000 in generative AI services for scanning and reconnaissance script development and uses OpenCode to manage models. This is a criminal group industrialising reconnaissance, which shortens the window between exposure and exploitation for everyone.

vulnerabilities.title: NGINX2Root Held Down a Second Day: 9.48 Million Exposed Services Against 74,782 Seen Fixed, Still No KEV Listing and Still No Confirmed Exploitation - and Rapid7's Own PoC README Explains Why Mass Exploitation Has Not Happened
affected_products: NGINX Open Source - fixed in 1.30.7 (stable) and 1.31.9 (mainline), both released 18 November 2026
NGINX Plus - check F5 advisory for the corresponding builds
Ubuntu 24.04 - distribution patch available as of 19 November 2026
Vulnerable component: HTTP/2 processing (CVE-2026-123007, CVSS v4.0 9.2)
Five CVEs total in the NGINX2Root set
Related but unpatched: a Linux kernel SCTP flaw completing the chain to root, with no CVE and no upstream patch
vulnerabilities.summary:
Held at a deliberately low rank for a second consecutive day, and this run can finally explain why the predicted mass exploitation has not materialised - which is more useful than another week of 'no confirmed exploitation yet'.

The numbers that justify the rank. Censys reports 9,482,482 exposed nginx services on its most recent scans, against just 74,782 observed as fixed at one point in its tracking - a remediation rate well under one percent, though that fixed figure may be dated. None of the five NGINX2Root CVEs appears in CISA's KEV catalogue. No confirmed in-the-wild exploitation has been reported as of approximately 20 November. That combination - the largest exposed population in this entire report, and the least evidence of anyone actually using it - is exactly why it sits at rank 9 rather than rank 1, and it is a useful corrective to the instinct that exposure count equals priority.

The explanation, which is the new material. Rapid7's Stephen Fewer published a technical analysis and a proof-of-concept exploit for CVE-2026-123007, and the PoC's own README warns that it 'will likely fail against a vulnerable NGINX server which has multiple concurrent clients'. That single sentence accounts for the quiet. A memory corruption exploit that depends on predictable heap state will not survive a busy production web server, and nginx's defining characteristic is handling many concurrent connections. The exposed population of 9.48 million is overwhelmingly busy production servers. Reliable mass exploitation therefore requires either a materially better exploit or a different technique, and other researchers - Xint among them - state they have working exploits but are deliberately withholding the final steps. The risk here is not that exploitation is impossible; it is that someone with a better heap grooming technique publishes, and the picture changes within a day. Treat the current quiet as a reprieve, not an outcome.

The escalation chain is the part that remains genuinely unaddressed, and it has not improved. The route to root is completed by a Linux kernel SCTP flaw that still has no CVE identifier and no upstream patch. That means you cannot scan for it, you cannot patch it, and you cannot track it in a vulnerability management tool. What you can do takes five minutes: blacklist the SCTP kernel module on any server that does not use it, which is nearly all of them. This feed has recommended that on each of the last three runs and it remains the single highest-value five-minute action in this report. It removes the privilege escalation stage of the chain for a module almost nobody needs, and unlike the nginx patch it requires no service restart negotiation.

The CVE numbering conflict needs resolving locally before you write a change record. Most sources name CVE-2026-123007 as the lead flaw; watchtowr labels CVE-2026-123633 as 'the' NGINX2root CVE. Both identifiers are in the five-CVE set, and both are fixed by the same releases, so for remediation purposes the distinction does not matter - but for ticket matching, scanner reconciliation and audit evidence it very much does. Pick the vendor advisory's numbering and be consistent.

UK relevance, stated honestly. There is no UK-specific angle to NGINX2Root, no UK victim, and no NCSC or NHS England alert that this run surfaced. It is in this report because nginx is the web server underneath a very large share of UK public sector and corporate web estate, because the exposed population is enormous, and because the remediation window is still open. It is at rank 9 because open remediation windows with no confirmed exploitation lose to three KEV deadlines falling inside 48 hours.

Confidence and caveats. High on the fixed versions 1.30.7 and 1.31.9 and their 18 November release, the CVSS v4.0 score of 9.2, the five-CVE grouping, the absence of all five from KEV, the existence of Rapid7's PoC and the content of its README caveat, the Ubuntu 24.04 patch availability, and the HTTP/2 disabling mitigation and its gRPC consequence. Medium on the Censys figures, which are point-in-time and whose 'fixed' count is explicitly noted as possibly dated. Medium on the absence of exploitation, which is a statement about the absence of public reporting rather than a statement about reality. The kernel SCTP flaw having no CVE and no patch is carried from previous runs and was not re-verified in this window.
recommended_actions: Blacklist the SCTP kernel module on every server that does not explicitly use it. This takes five minutes, needs no service restart negotiation, and removes the privilege escalation stage of the chain - which has no CVE, no patch and no scanner coverage. It remains the highest-value five-minute action in this report.

Patch nginx to 1.30.7 (stable) or 1.31.9 (mainline). Both released 18 November. On Ubuntu 24.04 the distribution patch has been available since 19 November. Prioritise internet-facing instances, then internal ones.

If you cannot patch immediately, disable HTTP/2 on affected listening ports. This blocks both CVE-2026-123007 and CVE-2026-123633. Test first: services that require HTTP/2, notably gRPC, will stop working.

Do not treat the absence of confirmed exploitation as an outcome. Rapid7's PoC fails against servers with multiple concurrent clients, which is why the 9.48 million exposed services are mostly quiet - but other researchers hold working exploits and are withholding them. A better heap grooming technique changes this within a day.

Resolve the CVE numbering locally before writing change records. Most sources lead on CVE-2026-123007; watchtowr labels CVE-2026-123633 as the NGINX2root CVE. Both are in the five-CVE set and both are fixed by the same releases, but inconsistent identifiers break scanner reconciliation and audit evidence.

Measure your own remediation rate against the sector picture. Censys observed under one percent of exposed nginx services as fixed. If your own figure is comparable, the finding is about your patch pipeline for infrastructure software, not about this CVE.

Find the nginx instances that are not in your asset register - containers, appliance-embedded builds, reverse proxies deployed by application teams. These are the instances that will still be unpatched in six months, and the five-CVE set applies to them equally.
Re-check KEV status before downgrading this in your own tracking. None of the five CVEs is listed as of this run, and a KEV addition would be the signal that the exploitation picture has changed.

kql.name: nginx version inventory against the NGINX2Root fixed releases
kql.description: Remediation evidence. Extracts nginx version strings from syslog and classifies each against the fixed releases 1.30.7 and 1.31.9, so you can evidence the estate rather than estimate it.
kql.query:
let lookback = 30d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has "nginx"
| extend NginxVersion = extract(@"nginx/(\d+\.\d+\.\d+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| where isnotempty(NginxVersion)
| extend Parts = split(NginxVersion, ".")
| extend Major = toint(Parts[0]), Minor = toint(Parts[1]), Patch = toint(Parts[2])
| extend Status = case(
    Major == 1 and Minor == 30 and Patch >= 7, "patched-stable",
    Major == 1 and Minor == 31 and Patch >= 9, "patched-mainline",
    Major == 1 and Minor > 31, "likely-patched-verify",
    "VULNERABLE-NGINX2ROOT")
| summarize Hosts = make_set(Computer, 30), Sightings = count(), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by NginxVersion, Status
| order by Status asc, NginxVersion asc

kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csVersion has "2" or csProtocol has "HTTP/2"
| where scStatus in (400, 408, 431, 500, 502, 503)
| summarize Errors = count(), Statuses = make_set(scStatus, 10), Paths = dcount(csUriStem), UA = make_set(csUserAgent, 5)
    by cIP, bin(TimeGenerated, 10m)

kql.name: nginx worker process crashes and signal terminations
kql.description: The most reliable evidence of attempted memory corruption exploitation. Rapid7's PoC is noted as likely to fail against busy servers - failed attempts produce worker crashes, which are the signal to look for.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has "nginx" or ProcessName has "nginx"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("worker process", "signal", "SIGSEGV", "SIGABRT", "core dumped", "exited on signal", "segfault")
| summarize Crashes = count(), Messages = make_set(SyslogMessage, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated)
    by Computer, bin(TimeGenerated, 1h)
| where Crashes > 2
| order by Crashes desc

kql.name: SCTP kernel module presence and loading
kql.description: Targets the unpatchable escalation stage. The SCTP flaw completing the chain to root has no CVE and no upstream patch, so module presence is the only control. Surfaces SCTP module load events and socket creation on hosts that should not have it.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("sctp", "SCTP")
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("module", "loaded", "insmod", "modprobe", "socket", "registered")
| summarize Events = count(), Messages = make_set(SyslogMessage, 10), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen = max(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| order by Events desc

kql.name: Privilege escalation and post-exploitation from the nginx worker context
kql.description: Catches the chain completing. An nginx worker process spawning shells, interpreters or module-loading utilities indicates successful exploitation followed by escalation attempts.
kql.query:

DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has "nginx"
| where FileName in~ ("sh", "bash", "dash", "python", "python3", "perl", "curl", "wget", "modprobe", "insmod", "gcc", "cc", "nc", "socat", "chmod")

vulnerabilities.title: The Deadline and Evidence-Quality Board: Five KEV Deadlines Inside 48 Hours, One KEV Entry With No Published Evidence At All, N-able's Hotfix 3 Contradicted by a Reported Working Exploit Chain, and the One Item This Run Can Close
vulnerabilities.vendor: Multiple - SAP, OpenBSD, GPUStack, SignalWire, IBM, Perforce, Apache, N-able, Optimizely
affected_products: SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal - CVE-2025-42884, JNDI injection, KEV deadline 23 November, SAP Note 3660969
OpenSSH before 10.6p2 on Linux using musl libc without PAM - CVE-2026-123158 'SSHole', CVSS 8.1; Alpine default server configuration affected; glibc distributions reported unaffected
GPUStack - CVE-2026-102895, unauthenticated admin-level access, fixed in 2.2.0
SignalWire FreeSWITCH 1.11.2 and earlier - CVE-2026-116779, CVSS 9.8 SIP MESSAGE command injection, fixed in 1.11.3
IBM Aspera Faspex - CVE-2026-123218, CVSS 9.8 incorrect authorization, fixed in 5.0.19 PL1
Perforce Puppet Enterprise - CVE-2026-115731, deserialisation, KEV 17 November
Apache Axis - CVE-2026-90436, KEV deadline was 21 November; no vendor fix
N-able N-central - 33 disclosed zero-days ('Able2Shell'); 2026.4 Hotfix 2 (10 November), Hotfix 3 (16 November)
Optimizely Web Experimentation - OPTIMJACK supply chain compromise, 16 November
vulnerabilities.summary:
The housekeeping entry, and this week it carries a theme rather than just a list: the evidence behind authoritative exploitation claims is inconsistent enough that 'it is in KEV' and 'we applied the hotfix' have both stopped being sufficient answers.

THE DEADLINE BOARD. Monday 23 November: VMware vCenter CVE-2026-123890 (rank 1), Cisco Expressway CVE-2026-76466 (rank 3), Apache Roller CVE-2026-129448 (rank 5) and SAP NetWeaver CVE-2025-42884. Tuesday 24 November: Microsoft Outlook CVE-2026-124194 (rank 4). Already passed: Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 on 21 November, with no vendor fix available at all - which makes it a permanent risk acceptance rather than an overdue patch, and it should be recorded as such; the GPUStack, FreeSWITCH, OpenSSH and IBM Aspera Faspex batch on 12 November; Perforce Puppet Enterprise CVE-2026-115731, added 17 November. Five deadlines inside 48 hours is an unusual concentration and it is the practical reason this report leads with three patching entries.

SAP NETWEAVER IS THE EVIDENCE PROBLEM IN ITS PUREST FORM. CVE-2025-42884 is an unauthenticated JNDI injection in SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal, CVSS 6.5, fixed by SAP in November 2025 under SAP Note 3660969. CISA added it to KEV on 20 November 2026 with a 23 November deadline. And yet: no indicators of compromise, no threat actor attribution and no proof-of-concept exploit code have been published by SAP, CISA or Onapsis, and one source states that no public reports document exploitation of this flaw at all. So a year-old patch has acquired a three-day federal deadline on the strength of evidence that nobody outside CISA can see. The right response is still to apply SAP Note 3660969 - it has been available for a year and there is no reason not to - but if you are being asked to justify emergency change control on this, be clear that the justification is CISA's unpublished evidence, not anything you can point to. A ZoomEye search reportedly returns 71,948 fingerprint matches for the product, which is a reachability figure, not a vulnerable count.

N-ABLE: THE HOTFIX CONTRADICTION, WHICH MATTERS TO EVERY UK MSP CUSTOMER. The sequence: 33 alleged zero-days with exploit code published by an independent researcher on 9 November; N-able took hosted N-central environments offline and told on-premises customers to shut servers down; Hotfix 2 on 10 November; all hosted NCOD servers upgraded across every region by 01:04 UTC on 11 November; Hotfix 3 on 16 November, with legacy APIs now permanently blocked in updated environments. N-able has consistently stated no evidence of successful exploitation in customer environments. But Field Effect reports that researchers consider the 10 November hotfix did not fully resolve the issue, that a further exploit chain reported to work against N-central 2026.4 HF2 (build 2026.4.1.26) was released, and that reporting indicates production servers have been compromised and used to deploy an XMRig cryptocurrency miner. Watchtower and Defused reported probing of N-central honeypots. Those two accounts cannot both be right. If you are a UK organisation served by an MSP running N-central, the question to ask your provider this week is specific: are you on Hotfix 3, and have you hunted for XMRig and for persistence, rather than relying on the vendor's statement that no exploitation occurred. Note also that organisations behind Mail Assure or SpamExperts retain the 16-20 November email forensic gap recorded in the 21 November run.

OPENSSH 'SSHOLE' CVE-2026-123158 - THE ITEM MOST LIKELY TO BE PRESENT AND UNNOTICED. The mechanism is elegant and worth understanding: an oversized password between 257 and 1,024 bytes makes musl's hashing fail and return '*', which sshd then accepts for accounts whose password field is locked. No real credentials needed. It affects OpenSSH before 10.6p2 on Linux systems using musl libc without PAM - which is Alpine Linux's default server configuration, and therefore an enormous number of containers. glibc distributions (Ubuntu, Debian, Fedora, Red Hat) are reported unaffected, as are key-only configurations. Exploitation began under nine hours after publication; Previdian confirmed root on an Alpine honeypot and logged 26 attempts from 17 IPs across 12 countries between 6 and 10 November; follow-on activity includes TAC Agent malware, botnet enrolment and cryptomining. CISA added it on 9 November; the deadline passed on 12 November. The reason it belongs here rather than in a closed file is that most organisations assess SSH exposure against their server estate, not against their container base images, and Alpine is the default base image for a very large share of CI pipelines.

THE ONE ITEM THIS RUN CAN CLOSE. Yesterday's run flagged that TalkTalk was reportedly the last organisation whose Optimizely snippet still contained the OPTIMJACK malware. That is resolved: Report URI states all infected Optimizely files were clean by 21:52 UTC on 16 November and have remained clean since, with every monitored file clean by 23:11. Optimizely has patched the flaw, removed the injected code, revoked tokens and notified affected customers. Two caveats remain. The 178 organisations figure is exposure, not confirmed breach - Scott Helme stated explicitly that it represents potentially affected websites rather than 178 confirmed corporate breaches. And the single most instructive detail for UK organisations stands: HSBC's content security policy blocked the main malicious script, but a backup copy still ran. A CSP that stops the primary payload and not the fallback is a partial control that will be recorded as a successful one. Report URI checked 1,611 snippets and found 188 infected across 178 organisations, including Optimizely's own website and login portal; researchers say the true number is likely higher because only a sample could be checked. UK names in the affected set include the BBC, TalkTalk and O2.

Confidence and caveats. High on all deadline dates, the SAP Note number, the OpenSSH mechanism and affected configuration, the N-able hotfix chronology, and the Optimizely remediation timestamps. Medium on the Field Effect compromise and XMRig claims, which are single-source and contradicted by the vendor. Low on SAP NetWeaver exploitation, where the KEV listing is the only evidence and it is unpublished. Several results in this run were GitHub issue bots and aggregators rather than primary sources, and no direct page fetch succeeded - verify KEV entries against CISA's catalogue directly before relying on the dates for audit purposes.
recommended_actions: Work the deadline board in order. Monday 23 November: vCenter, Cisco Expressway, Apache Roller, SAP NetWeaver. Tuesday 24 November: Outlook. Five deadlines inside 48 hours is why this report leads with patching rather than analysis.

Record Apache Axis CVE-2026-90436 as a formal risk acceptance, not an overdue patch. Its KEV deadline passed on 21 November and there is no vendor fix. An item with no available remediation needs a documented decision and a compensating control, not a recurring ticket.

kql.name: SAP NetWeaver Enterprise Portal JNDI injection attempts
kql.description: Detection for CVE-2025-42884 despite no public IOCs existing. Surfaces JNDI and LDAP lookup markers in requests to SAP portal paths - the structural signature of JNDI injection regardless of specific payload.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/irj", "/portal", "/webdynpro", "/sap/", "/NetWeaver", "/nwa")
| where csUriQuery has_any ("jndi:", "ldap:", "ldaps:", "rmi:", "iiop:", "dns:", "${", "%24%7B")
    or csUriStem has_any ("jndi", "${")
| project TimeGenerated, cIP, csMethod, csUriStem, csUriQuery, scStatus, csUserAgent, sSiteName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

kql.name: OpenSSH SSHole oversized password authentication bypass
kql.description: Detection for CVE-2026-123158. The mechanism requires a password of 257 to 1,024 bytes, which produces abnormally large authentication requests. Surfaces sshd authentication anomalies and accepted logins for locked accounts on musl-based hosts.
kql.query:
let lookback = 60d;
Syslog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where ProcessName has "sshd" or SyslogMessage has "sshd"
| where SyslogMessage has_any ("Accepted password", "authentication failure", "error: PAM", "Invalid user", "maximum authentication attempts", "input_userauth_request")
| extend SrcIP = extract(@"from ([0-9]{1,3}(?:\.[0-9]{1,3}){3})", 1, SyslogMessage)
| extend User = extract(@"(?:for|user) ([A-Za-z0-9._\-]+)", 1, SyslogMessage)
| summarize Events = count(), Accepted = countif(SyslogMessage has "Accepted"), Users = make_set(User, 15), Msgs = make_set(SyslogMessage, 5)
    by Computer, SrcIP
| where Accepted > 0 or Events > 20
| order by Accepted desc, Events desc

kql.name: XMRig cryptominer and post-exploitation on N-central and managed infrastructure
kql.description: Tests the Field Effect claim directly rather than relying on the vendor's no-exploitation statement. Surfaces cryptomining process and command-line indicators on RMM and managed infrastructure hosts.

let lookback = 60d;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(lookback)
| where FileName has_any ("xmrig", "minerd", "cpuminer", "nbminer", "ethminer", "kinsing")
    or ProcessCommandLine has_any ("--donate-level", "stratum+tcp", "stratum+ssl", "--coin=monero", "randomx", "nicehash", "pool.minexmr", "xmrpool")

kql.name: N-central legacy API access after Hotfix 3
kql.description: Hotfix 3 (16 November) permanently blocks legacy APIs in updated environments. Any successful legacy API call after upgrade indicates either an incomplete upgrade or a bypass - which is exactly the contested claim.
kql.query:
let lookback = 45d;
W3CIISLog
| where TimeGenerated > ago(lookback)
| where csUriStem has_any ("/dms", "/dms2", "/api/", "/ncentral", "/deviceasset", "/sessionservice", "/ServerEI", "/ServerEI2")

kql.name: FreeSWITCH SIP MESSAGE command injection and GPUStack unauthenticated access
